rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Islahi has explained the similarity between adultery and polytheism elsewhere in the exegesis, so he does not repeat that discussion here.
rows.anchor: been referring to the similarity between adultery and polytheism at many places of this exegesis. Repetition thus is not required here.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The fourth pledge directive prohibits killing children; it covers infanticide driven by jāhiliyyah superstition, poverty, false honour, and motives arising in the present age.
rows.anchor: The fourth directive is that they will not kill their children:

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Islahi reads the phrase about what lies between hands and feet as a polite euphemism for sexual organs, comprehensively covering sexual accusations and advances.
rows.anchor: In my opinion, these words refer to the sexual organs. These organs are located between the hands and the feet.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The euphemism alludes to accusations related to sex, including adultery and sexual advances such as kissing and fondling.
rows.anchor: In a very decent manner, it alludes to all the accusations which relate to sex, like adultery and sexual advances like kissing and fondling.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Sexual accusations gravely attack reputation and may provoke uncontrollable conflict; they are sinful for men and women, but women are especially warned because defence against their accusations is difficult.
rows.anchor: a sexual accusation by a woman is a very grave attack, against which defence is extremely difficult.

rows.speaker: Our exegetes
rows.claim: Exegetes generally take the phrase to forbid a woman from attributing to her husband a pregnancy caused by another man.
rows.anchor: Our exegetes have generally interpreted these words to mean that a woman should not attribute her pregnancy caused by some other man to her husband.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Islahi rejects limiting the phrase to disputed paternity and applies it broadly to everything covered by its wording.
rows.anchor: I have interpreted them in a wider sense above so that their sphere of application includes everything which should come under them.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The sixth directive requires women not to disobey the Prophet in any maʿrūf; prior pledges detail avoidance of munkar, while prayer, fasting, pilgrimage, justice, and fairness fall under familiar maʿrūf obligations.
rows.anchor: All the previously mentioned things relate to what is munkar. They do not relate to what is ma‘rūf like the prayer, the fast, the ḥajj and justice and fairness.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Because many women entering Islam after the conquest of Makkah had been involved in the listed jāhiliyyah sins, the pledge details abstention from munkar but states adherence to maʿrūf generally.
rows.anchor: This special situation entailed that the pledge of refraining from the munkarāt (plural of munkar) be taken from them in detail

rows.speaker: Some people
rows.claim: Some interpreters treat the phrase as conditional and infer that obedience to the Prophet is limited to commands that accord with maʿrūf.
rows.anchor: Some people have interpreted the words 8 9 as a conditional phrase

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Qur'an repeatedly ends sūrahs on the subject with which they began, and Islahi presents this recurring pattern as a strong argument for coherence.
rows.anchor: This fact, in itself, is a great argument for the existence of coherence in the Qur’ān.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The opening forbids befriending God's enemies; earlier musabbiḥāt sūrahs describe Jewish conspiracies and direct Muslims to keep away from the Jews and their associates.
rows.anchor: The musabbiḥāt sūrahs, which have preceded this sūrah, mention mostly the conspiracies of the Jews and their compatriots

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Islahi calls this inference far-fetched: a divinely protected Prophet cannot direct people to munkar, always directs them to maʿrūf, and is the measure of good and evil, so obeying him is essential to faith.
rows.anchor: directs his people to do anything munkar, nor is he capable of doing it.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The only meaningful condition on a covenant taken by the Prophet is each person's strength and capacity, which narratives show he would remind people of.
rows.anchor: strength and capacity, and it is evident from certain narratives that the Prophet (sws)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Pledges taken by the Prophet's Companions or successors must be conditional on maʿrūf, since they could direct people against it; after the Prophet, no one may demand absolute obedience.
rows.anchor: no one has the right to take a pledge of absolute obedience from people.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Narratives describe several forms of the women's pledge, but Islahi regards it as certain that the Prophet never took their hands while accepting it.
rows.anchor: evident from them is that the Prophet (sws) never took their hands in his own when he was taking this pledge.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse directs the Prophet to make the covenant with women who will avoid munkar and uphold maʿrūf, and to seek God's forgiveness so their past blemishes may be forgiven through His mercy.
rows.anchor: blemishes are forgiven by Him. This is because He is Forgiving and Merciful; He will have mercy on them.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Friendship with Jews or idolaters cannot benefit Muslims: Islahi says the two groups share the same level of belief, practice, and fate, and their ally will share their devastation.
rows.anchor: Both these denominations are of the same level as far as their beliefs and practices are concerned, and are going to meet the same fate as well.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The description of people who incurred God's wrath can refer only to Jews, since the Qur'an uses this attribute for them, as in al-Fātiḥah.
rows.anchor: obviously can only refer to the Jews. The attribute they mention is used for them only by the Qur’ ān.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Although Jews acknowledge the Hereafter, worldly attachment, greed, and evasion of death show they do not expect it; otherwise they would heed God's severe warnings and abandon their conduct.
rows.anchor: their infatuation for worldly pleasures, their greed for wealth and their escapism from death, all bear witness that they do not expect the Hereafter to happen.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The comparison says idolaters do not expect their dead to rise, as expressed in Qāf 50:3, and Jews show the same lack of expectation about the Hereafter.
rows.anchor: when we are dead and turned to dust? Such a return is most-improbable! (50:3)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Qur'an repeatedly compares Jews and idolaters to dispel Muslims' optimism about Jews as People of the Book and show that neither group is better than the other.
rows.anchor: the Qur’ ān has brought to the fore the similarity between these two religious groups

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The seventh and final Qur'anic group begins with al-Mulk and follows the prior groups' order: Makkan sūrahs precede a few Madinan ones, which branch from the Makkan stem.
rows.anchor: The sūrahs of this group too are arranged in the same manner as they are arranged in the previous ones.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Because the Makkan or Madinan identity of some sūrahs is disputed, Islahi gives only a preliminary estimate: al-Mulk through al-Kāfirūn are 43 Makkan sūrahs, followed by Madinan al-Nāṣr through al-Nās.
rows.anchor: Nāṣr to Sūrah al-Nās are Madīnan.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Like previous groups, this group discusses monotheism, prophethood, and the Hereafter, and contains the phases of preaching.
rows.anchor: the fundamentals of the Qur’ ānic message: monotheism, prophethood and the hereafter have been discussed

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The group's real subject is warning; most sūrahs are early Makkan, using the warning style Muhammad adopted at Ṣafā.
rows.anchor: the style of indhār adopted in them is the same as was adopted by Muḥammad (sws) atop the hillock of Ṣafā.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: As warning, the group vividly portrays Judgment and the necessary punishment for rejecting a Messenger, as if Quraysh witnessed it themselves.
rows.anchor: the punishment which necessarily comes as a result of rejecting a Messenger of God is depicted in such a maner as if the Quraysh

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The arguments rest on established historical facts and manifest signs in the human world and the world around it.
rows.anchor: The arguments used are based on established facts of history and manifest signs found in the worlds within man and the one around him.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Islahi likens the force of the group's discourse to thunder and lightning that shakes its listeners.
rows.anchor: The force in the discourse is like the roar of thunder and the bolt of lightning that shakes and jolts everyone.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The sūrahs stirred all Arabia so that people became either Qur'an's fierce enemies or advocates.
rows.anchor: Such was the upheaval caused by these sūrahs in the whole of Arabia that not a single person remained neutral about the message of the Qur’ ān

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Their conflict culminated in truth's dominance, a result also noted at the end of every group and this one.
rows.anchor: the dominance of the truth which is mentioned at the end of every group

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Islahi cites al-Ḥijr 15:87, which calls the Qur'an seven mathānī, to support that its division into seven groups is sanctioned by the Qur'an itself.
rows.anchor: While beginning the exegesis of the seventh group, I would like to cite the following verse of

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Islahi argues that the Qur'an does not designate a specific sūrah as sabʿ mathānī; 39:23 instead shows the whole Qur'an is described as mathānī.
rows.anchor: Firstly, the Qur’ān has not called any specific sūrah as the sab‘ mathāni.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: He argues that mathānī means paired occurrences, rather than something repeated frequently.
rows.anchor: Secondly, the word mathānī does not refer to something which is often repeated; it refers to something which occurs in pairs.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: He argues that the Qur'an's arrangement divides it into seven groups with sūrahs occurring in pairs.
rows.anchor: the sūrahs in the Qur’ ān that they are divided into seven groups and sūrahs occur in pairs

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: He invites readers to assess whether these premises are convincing and whether the proposed arrangement has opened new fields of knowledge.
rows.anchor: the reader that he can now judge whether what is said in these points holds water or not

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Islahi takes Ibn Masʿūd's report from the Prophet that the Qur'an was revealed on seven aḥruf to point to the Qur'an's arrangement into seven groups.
rows.anchor: ‘Abdullāh Ibn Mas‘ūd (rta) reported from the Prophet (sws) points to

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: He rejects the interpretation that seven aḥruf means every Qur'anic word has seven readings; this would make the Qur'an an enigma despite its description as lucid Arabic and the Quraysh's pure language.
rows.anchor: the Qur’ ān would become an enigma, even though as per its own words it is revealed in lucid Arabic, and the pure language of the Quraysh

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: As an empirical argument against seven readings per word, he notes that even Ibn Jarīr, despite generously citing variants, is not remembered as giving more than two or three readings of a word.
rows.anchor: Ibn Jar īr has generously quoted variant readings, yet I do not remember him quoting more than two or three readings of a word.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Islahi says most apparent reading differences are interpretive: an early authority's explanatory word could be mistaken for a variant reading of the Qur'anic word.
rows.anchor: Further deliberation shows that difference in readings is not in fact a difference in readings; most of it relates to difference in interpretation.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: He gives fa-qad ṣaghat read as fa-qad zāghat as an example of an explanatory gloss misreported as a reading, and says classical Arabic shows the proposed meaning is wrong.
rows.anchor: It was clear that this word was not a new reading of the word; it was only meant to explain it.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Only the mutawātir reading found among people and in every ummah codex counts as established; all other readings are shādhdh and should not be privileged over it.
rows.anchor: all other readngs are not not mutawātir and are shādh (rare), and cannot be given importance to, in the presence of the mutawātir reading.
